en: The Pure Land of Pure Lapis Lazuli represents the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguru Vaidūryaprabha. His entire body is a light blue color.
Within a jeweled cave, upon a lotus flower made of a hundred jewels, the Master sits in the Great Emptiness Samādhi, emitting countless rays of light, each ray...
Within [this],
the innumerable emanated bodies of the Buddhas all possess the characteristics of the Great Emptiness Samādhi.
With the right arm raised and the palm facing upward, extend the fingers like opening petals;
place the left hand below the navel with the little finger hooked inward.
This is called the Great Jewel Lapis Lazuli Medicine.
Its ground is the color of deep blue lapis lazuli,
with countless jewel-flower trees as numerous as motes of dust;
the shapes of the trees' flowers and leaves [are as follows].
Or it may take the form of a Buddha,
emitting immeasurable light;
this is called the Buddha-pāramitā.
Or appearing in the form of a bodhisattva,
they produce immeasurable music;
this is called the samādhi of dhāraṇī.
Or it has the form of a golden hall,
emitting immeasurable clouds of hundreds of jewels,
named "Sublime Array of Bodhi."
Some are in the shape of jeweled stupas,
from which immeasurable hosts of devas are born;
they are called the Tree of Awakening Wisdom, the Desert Sun Rain-Wheel Tree, and the Island of Tides, where hundreds of thousands of banners of merit and wisdom are arrayed in rows.
It was adorned with immeasurable jeweled nets, jeweled garlands, bells, and so forth.

To the left and right of the Buddha, members of the four castes who had gone forth from the household life all entered meditative absorption—namely, kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders. In the first row to the left, there appeared the Bodhisattva Vajragarbharāja.
The Bodhisattva’s entire body is a light reddish-blue color.
He sits upon a precious lotus pedestal;
in the center of his right palm, he holds a three-pronged vajra.
The left arm is bent with the five fingers interlaced above;
the thumb presses down upon the nail of the little finger,
serving as the retinue of dust-mote-like bodhisattvas.
These are the Bodhisattvas known as Cloud Fragrance,
Flower-Jewel, and Vajra-Palms-Joined.
The Bodhisattvas Agnīśvararūpa and Ṛṣirūpa, and so forth;
on the first tier to the right is Padmadhvaja-vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva.
His entire body is a light blue color.
He sits upon a precious lotus flower pedestal,
holding a cintāmaṇi jewel in his left hand.
Upon a white jewel lotus pedestal is placed a vajra.
His right hand forms the varada-mudrā with the middle finger bent; he is attended by a host of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust, namely the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus.
There are Bodhisattvas holding a three-pronged vajra and Bodhisattvas holding a single-pronged vajra bell, and so forth.
On the second tier to the left is the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha.
The entire body is crimson red;
the palm of the left hand rests upon the sun disk,
and the right hand holds a *mañjūṣaka* flower that is deep vermilion in appearance.
Some are fully blossomed,
some are half-open,
and some are yet unopened.
Or perhaps it was made of precious fruit.
Countless bodhisattvas served as his attendants,
namely bodhisattvas such as those holding incense burners and those holding mahāmanjūṣaka flowers and other red blossoms.
To the right, in the second tier, is the Bodhisattva Candraprabha.
His entire body is white with a reddish tint; his left hand holds a lunar disc, and his right hand grasps a red-and-white lotus flower.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust served as his attendants,
namely Bodhisattvas such as Āṅkuśadhara and Ghaṇṭādhara,
who stood near the Tathāgata’s rear.
He manifests as ten disciples and twenty-one, thirty-five, or other numbers of arhats, each with an immeasurable assembly of śrāvakas as their retinue.

The leaders each take up objects according to their original forms and mudrās; their respective retinues remain on the right to uphold the Dharma-forms, while those on the left, rear, and front manifest as immeasurable sages and celestial maidens, holding seasonal flowers.
To the left and right of the Buddha, in the outer courtyard,
there are forms of the music and dance of immeasurable celestial hosts;
that is to say, the appearance of kinnarīs offering lutes and celestial music.
The kinnaras have the appearance of playing golden drums from their own hearts;
the garuḍa maidens have the appearance of playing flutes and celestial music;
and the earth goddesses all have the appearance of playing drums and musical instruments.
The asura maidens presented the appearance of offering celestial drums and music;
the mahoraga maidens presented the appearance of offering the sheng flute and music;
and the host of deities from the great māra’s retinue presented the appearance of offering celestial dance and music.
In the outer courtyard, above, below, and in the eight directions,
there are the assemblies of the twelve divine generals,
with countless hosts of *vajra*-youths as their retinue.
Regarding the forms of the twelve divine generals:
the first is the Great General Viśākha Īśāna, who is formidable;
he is yellow in color and rides a tiger.
Holding a khadga sword,
with the right hand in a fist pressed against the left hip;
some say he faces the northeast.
The second is the Great Vajra General Vajrendra,
who is blue in color with red eyes, riding upon a bull,
and holding a three-pronged vajra.
The left hand is bent with the palm facing upward;
some say this represents the East.
Third is the Great General Mahāpāla of the Quarter of Maitrīlaghaṇa.
Its color is blue with upward-flaming smoke, mounted upon a dragon;
it holds a flaming spear and a banner in its two hands, which are poised.
Some say it belongs to the southeast direction.
The fourth is the Great General Anīlāgaja,
whose color is yellowish-red with upward-flaming smoke,
who rides upon a serpent and wields a *caṇḍa* axe.
With the left hand in a fist, extend the index finger (the wind-finger); this is the fire-jewel.
Alternatively, it is said that one forms [the mudrā] of the South.
Fifth, place at the bottom the Great General of the Square Dharma, Yamāntaka.
His color is red; he emits blazing thunder from his eyes and fire from his hair; he is mounted upon two winged horses.
In his left hand he holds a *daiyuelu*, and in his right he holds a mirror atop flames.
Some say he is located in the southwest.
He is the sixth great general of the rākṣasas, Sandhira-nirghātin,
who is yellowish-red in color, has the form of a rākṣasa, and rides upon a ram.
Holding a mirror in the left hand and a khadga sword in the right;
alternatively, one may hold a daṇḍa-śakti,
or it is said that one should form the mudrā of the western direction.
The seventh is the Great General Indrāṇī, the Queen of the North-East;
she is yellow in color, rides upon a camel,
and holds a white fly-whisk in her left hand.
The one on the right holds a bell to cause [the deity] to gaze [upon him].
Some say he represents the western or northern direction.
The eighth is the Great General of the Wolves, the Dragon of the *Vaimatya* (跋伊羅) region.
His color is white; he is mounted upon a golden-winged bird (garuḍa).
In his left hand he holds a wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), and in his right hand he holds a vajra-bell.
Some say he is the ninth Mahoraga general of the north, while others call him the Great General of the Wind (Vāyu).
The mount has the form of a dog and is fearsome;
it is what is called a *tengou* (celestial dog).
Its left fist extends toward the wheel of the wind.
The Wind of Rightward Bending is black in color, like a black wind;
some say it presides over the zenith.
The tenth is Tridaśabhaṅga, the Great General who subdues water in the northwest.
Riding upon a boar, he holds a hook in his right hand and bends the earth and water with his left; his color is like black water.
Some say this represents the lower direction.
The eleventh is the invitation of Dūrasvāmin, the World-Protecting General of the Vaiśravaṇa direction.
Furthermore, the Great General Maṇi rides upon a rat and holds a cintāmaṇi jewel in his right hand.
He holds a noose in his left hand;
his color is like that of a black cloud on a summer day.
Some say he is to be depicted as belonging to the western direction.
The twelfth, the Great General Vighnarāja Īśāna of the northeast,
rides upon a bull— that is, a water buffalo—
and holds a precious bow and arrow in his hands.
Its color is blackish-blue;
it merely slightly diminishes the preceding color.
Some say it is the direction of the pass (guān).
In the presence of the Buddha, he was transformed into a kalaviṅka and a white swan.
These birds are the foremost among the five classes of superior beings; the sounds of the Dharma they preach are all identical, uttered with a single voice.
Therefore, they are called "birds of shared life" (sahajīvin).
The report regarding the Pure Lapis Lazuli Land has been completed.
This was transcribed on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month of the second year of Chōtei, after two revisions. Finished.
